topic: Day 1 · Defining & Staging AKI — KDIGO, Creatinine & Biomarkers
speakerBio: Nephrologist-intensivist who runs the hospital's electronic AKI-alert system and campaigns for the urine-output chart to be read as carefully as the biochemistry.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

It is 2 a.m. on the surgical ward. A 68-year-old man, two days post laparotomy, has passed only 90 mL of urine since midday. His creatinine this morning was 88 µmol/L — "normal," said the day team — and the night bloods are not back yet. The nurse asks whether she should "just give him a bag of fluid and review in the morning." Here is the trap you must not fall into: by the time his creatinine finally climbs above the lab's reference range, the injury will already be a day old. Creatinine is a trailing indicator — it reports yesterday's kidney. Tonight, the most sensitive AKI monitor in the hospital is not the biochemistry analyser; it is the urine output chart on the end of the bed. This session is about defining and staging AKI precisely — the KDIGO criteria, the three stages, why creatinine lies, and the biomarkers trying to replace it.

1 · 📏 Why we needed one definition — the birth of KDIGO

For decades "acute renal failure" meant whatever the writing consultant thought it meant, and studies could not be compared. The RIFLE (2004) and AKIN (2007) criteria narrowed it, and in 2012 KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) merged them into the single definition we still anchor on today. Its power is that it is deliberately sensitive: it catches injury early, using two independent tripwires — a change in serum creatinine and a fall in urine output — so that either can raise the alarm.

KDIGO is anchored on two tripwires: a rise in creatinine OR a fall in urine output. You only need ONE to diagnose AKI.

2 · ✅ The KDIGO diagnostic criteria — commit these to memory

AKI is diagnosed if any one of the following is present:

CriterionThresholdTime window
Absolute creatinine rise≥ 26.5 µmol/L (≥0.3 mg/dL)within 48 hours
Relative creatinine rise≥ 1.5 × baseline (a 50% rise)known/presumed within 7 days
Oliguriaurine output < 0.5 mL/kg/hfor ≥ 6 hours

Read those windows carefully, because they encode two different biological questions. The 48-hour, 26.5 µmol/L rule catches a sudden, absolute insult — the classic acute hit. The 7-day, 1.5× rule catches a proportionally significant, more gradual rise, and works even in a patient whose baseline is very low. A tiny woman with a baseline creatinine of 40 who climbs to 62 has met neither an alarm bell that a lazy eye would notice — 62 is "normal range" — yet she has had a 1.55× rise: that is stage 1 AKI, and KDIGO is built precisely to catch her.

💡 26.5, 1.5×, 0.5

Three numbers unlock the whole definition: 26.5 µmol/L absolute rise in 48h, 1.5× baseline in 7 days, urine output under 0.5 mL/kg/h. If you remember nothing else from this session, remember 26.5 – 1.5 – 0.5.

3 · 🪜 The three stages — severity by the worst criterion met

Once AKI is diagnosed, KDIGO stages it 1 to 3 by whichever criterion — creatinine or urine output — puts the patient in the highest bracket. Stage tracks mortality and the need for renal replacement almost linearly.

StageSerum creatinineUrine output
Stage 11.5–1.9× baseline, or ≥26.5 µmol/L absolute rise<0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h
Stage 22.0–2.9× baseline<0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 h
Stage 3≥3.0× baseline, or creatinine ≥353.6 µmol/L (≥4.0 mg/dL), or started on RRT (any age), or (if <18y) eGFR <35<0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 h, or anuria for ≥12 h

Two clinical shortcuts fall out of this table. First, starting dialysis makes it stage 3 by definition, regardless of the numbers that led you there. Second, the urine-output arm is stricter as you climb: stage 3 demands the deeper oliguria (<0.3 mL/kg/h) or frank anuria. Always stage on the worse of the two arms — a patient with only a stage-1 creatinine but 24 hours of <0.3 mL/kg/h output is stage 3.

🎯 Stage the patient, then act on the stage

Staging is not bureaucracy — it drives management. Stage 1 mandates a cause hunt, drug review and close monitoring. Stage 2–3 escalates to senior/renal review, consideration of the indications for RRT, and a hunt for reversible intrinsic causes. The stage is the shared language that gets the nephrologist out of bed.

4 · ⏳ Why creatinine lies — the trailing-indicator trap

Serum creatinine is cheap, universal, and deeply flawed as an acute marker. It is the product of muscle creatine breakdown, released at a near-constant rate and cleared by the kidney; its concentration reflects the balance of production and clearance. That makes it a lagging, context-dependent number in at least five ways:

LimitationMechanismClinical consequence
Kinetic lagCreatinine must accumulate before it crosses a threshold — even if GFR drops to zero, it rises only ~50–100 µmol/L per dayInjury is 24–48h old before the number moves; a falling creatinine may still mean a failing kidney if GFR only partly recovered
Muscle massLess muscle = less productionThe frail elderly, cachectic, amputees and cirrhotics have a low creatinine that overestimates GFR — a "normal" 70 can hide a badly impaired kidney
Sex & ethnicityDifferences in muscle massSame GFR gives different creatinine — why estimating equations correct for these
DilutionAggressive fluid resuscitation expands volume of distributionA resuscitated patient's creatinine can be diluted down, masking real injury
Tubular secretion & drugs~10–15% of creatinine is secreted, not filtered; trimethoprim, cimetidine, cobicistat block secretionThese raise creatinine and drop eGFR without any true fall in GFR — a pseudo-AKI
Creatinine is a trailing indicator — it reports the kidney of a day or two ago. A normal creatinine never rules out an evolving AKI tonight.
⚠️ The 'normal creatinine' in the sarcopenic patient

An 82-year-old, 48 kg woman with a creatinine of 75 does not have normal renal function — with her tiny muscle mass, that value may correspond to an eGFR in the 30s. Dose her gentamicin, her low-molecular-weight heparin, her DOAC or her contrast load on the assumption of a healthy kidney and you will overdose her. Always interpret creatinine against muscle mass, and when it matters, estimate GFR or measure cystatin C.

5 · 💧 The urine-output criterion — nuance the charts don't teach

Urine output is the real-time arm of KDIGO and often moves hours before creatinine, but it is riddled with practical traps:

  • It must be weight-indexed and hourly. "500 mL overnight" is meaningless without the patient's weight and the hours. For an 80 kg man, 0.5 mL/kg/h is 40 mL/h — 320 mL over 8 hours. Anything less is oliguric.
  • Oliguria is not always injury. A well person who is nil-by-mouth and antidiuretic overnight makes concentrated urine — appropriate physiology, not AKI. Conversely, non-oliguric AKI exists: some ATN and most nephrotoxic injury maintains urine volume while clearance collapses.
  • Anuria is a specific signal. Sudden, complete anuria points to a mechanical or vascular catastrophe — bilateral obstruction, a blocked catheter (always the first thing to exclude), renal artery/vein occlusion, or a cortical necrosis — rather than gradual ATN.
  • You need an accurate measure. Reliable hourly urine output in an unstable patient effectively requires a catheter; balance that against infection risk.
💡 Flush the catheter before you diagnose anuria

The commonest cause of "anuria" on a surgical ward is a blocked or kinked urinary catheter, not a dying kidney. A bladder scan and a catheter flush cost nothing and take two minutes — do them before you escalate an anuric patient as intrinsic AKI.

6 · 🧬 Novel biomarkers — trying to see the injury before creatinine rises

The holy grail is a "renal troponin": a marker that rises within hours of tubular injury, before creatinine has budged. Several are in clinical or research use, and they split into two mechanistic families — markers of damage and markers of stress:

BiomarkerWhat it reflectsTiming / role
NGAL (neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin)Up-regulated and released by injured tubular epitheliumRises within 2–6 h of tubular injury — a "damage" marker; studied in cardiac surgery & contrast AKI
Cystatin CA freely-filtered protein produced by all nucleated cells, independent of muscle massA better filtration marker than creatinine, especially in the sarcopenic; less kinetic lag
TIMP-2 · IGFBP7 (NephroCheck)Cell-cycle arrest markers — tubular cells enter G1 arrest ("hunker down") under stressPredicts moderate-severe AKI within 12 h; a "stress"/early-warning marker, FDA-cleared
KIM-1 (kidney injury molecule-1)Expressed on injured proximal tubuleMarker of established proximal tubular damage (mainly research)

The conceptual leap is the cell-cycle arrest idea behind TIMP-2·IGFBP7. When a tubular cell is stressed, it does not immediately die — it stops dividing and secretes these two proteins to protect itself, and they appear in the urine as an early alarm that injury is imminent, before any cell has actually necrosed and before creatinine climbs. That is why NephroCheck is marketed as a risk-stratifier ("is this patient about to develop AKI in the next 12 hours?") rather than a diagnostic.

🎯 Damage markers vs filtration markers vs stress markers

Sort the biomarkers by what they answer. Cystatin C answers "what is the true GFR right now?" (a better filtration marker). NGAL and KIM-1 answer "has the tubule been damaged?" (damage markers). TIMP-2·IGFBP7 answers "is this kidney stressed and about to fail?" (a pre-injury stress marker). Different questions, different clinical moments.

The honest caveat: none has yet replaced creatinine + urine output in routine practice or in the KDIGO definition itself. They refine risk and timing; they do not overturn the anchor. But they are how the field is escaping the trailing-indicator trap, and cystatin C in particular is already useful when muscle mass makes creatinine untrustworthy.

7 · 📐 Estimating the baseline — the number the whole definition depends on

Every KDIGO criterion is relative to a baseline creatinine, so a wrong baseline mis-stages the patient. Best to worst source:

  1. A real, recent, stable outpatient value (ideally 7–365 days old) — the gold standard.
  2. The lowest inpatient value during the admission — a reasonable surrogate when no prior result exists.
  3. Back-estimation from an assumed baseline eGFR (e.g. the MDRD-derived value assuming eGFR ~75) — a last resort that can badly misclassify, especially in the elderly.
No baseline, no reliable stage. Always chase a prior creatinine before you commit to a diagnosis of "new" AKI versus undiagnosed CKD.

The corollary matters clinically: a patient presenting with a creatinine of 300 and no prior results might have acute-on-chronic disease, established CKD mislabelled as AKI, or a genuine acute hit — small kidneys on ultrasound, anaemia and a raised phosphate hint at chronicity, while good-sized kidneys and a bland history hint at a reversible acute process.

☠️ M&M — the creatinine that was 'still in range'

A 34-year-old man with sepsis from pyelonephritis was admitted with a creatinine of 62 (his GP baseline, from a marathon-runner's medical, was 74 — high-normal for his large muscle mass). Over the next 36 hours he was aggressively fluid-resuscitated. His creatinine drifted up to 96, then 118 — each result flagged "normal" or only marginally high by the analyser, and the covering team, reading absolute values, were reassured. But 118 was already 1.6× his true baseline of 74 — stage 1, verging on stage 2 — and his urine output had been under 0.5 mL/kg/h for over 18 hours, quietly meeting stage 2 on its own. The dilutional effect of resuscitation had further blunted the apparent rise. Nephrology was called only when he became frankly oliguric at 48 hours, by which point he had established ATN and needed a week of dialysis. Lessons: stage against the patient's own baseline, not the lab reference range; a muscular young man's "normal" creatinine can hide a 60% rise; fluid resuscitation dilutes creatinine and masks injury; and the urine-output criterion had been screaming for a day while everyone watched the biochemistry. The chart on the end of the bed diagnosed the AKI a full day before the blood test admitted it.

8 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. KDIGO diagnoses AKI on any one of: creatinine rise ≥26.5 µmol/L in 48h, ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6h. Remember 26.5 – 1.5 – 0.5.
  2. Three stages, graded by the worse of the creatinine or urine-output arm; starting RRT is stage 3 by definition; stage tracks mortality and dialysis need.
  3. Creatinine is a trailing indicator — kinetic lag means the injury is a day or two old before it moves; a normal value never excludes an evolving AKI.
  4. Creatinine is distorted by muscle mass, sex, dilution and tubular-secretion-blocking drugs (trimethoprim, cimetidine) — interpret it against the individual, not the reference range.
  5. Urine output is the real-time arm: weight-index it hourly, exclude a blocked catheter before diagnosing anuria, and remember non-oliguric AKI exists.
  6. Biomarkers refine timing and risk: cystatin C (filtration, muscle-independent), NGAL/KIM-1 (damage), and TIMP-2·IGFBP7 / NephroCheck (cell-cycle-arrest stress marker predicting AKI within 12h) — none yet replaces the KDIGO anchor.
  7. The baseline creatinine underpins everything — chase a real prior value, or you will mis-stage and confuse acute injury with chronic disease.

moderatorQs.q: State the three KDIGO criteria for diagnosing AKI, and explain why two different creatinine thresholds with two different time windows are needed.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: AKI is present if any one holds: a creatinine rise of ≥26.5 µmol/L within 48 hours, a rise to ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 hours. The two creatinine rules ask different biological questions. The absolute 26.5 µmol/L over 48h rule detects a sudden, large insult and is robust regardless of baseline. The relative 1.5× over 7 days rule detects a proportionally significant but more gradual decline, and crucially catches patients with a very low baseline — a small woman going from 40 to 62 is still 'in range' on absolute terms but has a 1.55× rise, i.e. stage 1 AKI. Having both a proportional and an absolute tripwire, over both a short and a slightly longer window, is what makes KDIGO sensitive across the whole range of body sizes and tempos of injury.

moderatorQs.q: What does it mean to call creatinine a 'trailing indicator', and how does that change how you act on a normal result?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: It means creatinine reports the kidney of one to two days ago, not the kidney in front of you. Because creatinine has to accumulate before it crosses a threshold, even a GFR that has crashed to zero raises it only ~50–100 µmol/L per day — so there is an inevitable kinetic lag between the injury and the number moving, and a falling creatinine can still mask incomplete recovery. Practically, a 'normal' creatinine never rules out an evolving AKI tonight: I act on the trajectory and the context, not a single in-range value. I lean on the real-time signals instead — hourly weight-indexed urine output, the clinical picture of hypoperfusion or sepsis, the drug chart, and where available an early stress/damage biomarker — rather than waiting for the biochemistry to catch up and confirm damage that is already done.

moderatorQs.q: Explain the concept behind the cell-cycle-arrest biomarkers TIMP-2 and IGFBP7, and how their clinical use differs from creatinine.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: When a renal tubular cell is stressed — by ischaemia, sepsis or a nephrotoxin — it does not die immediately; it enters G1 cell-cycle arrest, effectively hunkering down to protect itself, and secretes two proteins, TIMP-2 and IGFBP7, into the urine. Their product (marketed as NephroCheck) therefore appears before any cell has necrosed and well before creatinine rises, so it functions as a pre-injury stress/early-warning marker: an elevated value flags a patient at high risk of developing moderate-to-severe AKI within the next ~12 hours. That is a fundamentally different clinical use from creatinine, which is a late, retrospective marker of filtration already lost. In practice it is a risk-stratifier prompting protective measures (optimise haemodynamics, stop nephrotoxins, avoid contrast) rather than a diagnostic — and it does not yet replace creatinine or urine output in the KDIGO definition itself.

audienceQs.q: The lab says my elderly patient's creatinine is 78, which is normal. Why is my registrar still worried about her kidneys?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because creatinine depends on muscle mass, and a frail, low-weight elderly woman produces very little of it. In her, a value of 78 that looks mid-range can correspond to an eGFR down in the 30s — the reference range was built on people with far more muscle. So the 'normal' number is overestimating her true GFR. That matters most for drug dosing: gentamicin, low-molecular-weight heparin, DOACs, metformin and a contrast load all need her real kidney function, and treating her as normal risks toxicity. Estimate her GFR (or, when it really matters, measure cystatin C, which is independent of muscle mass), interpret creatinine against her body habitus, and dose renally.

audienceQs.q: My patient's creatinine actually fell overnight after a big fluid resuscitation — can I relax about their kidneys?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Be careful — that fall may be dilutional rather than real recovery. Aggressive fluid resuscitation expands the volume of distribution and can dilute the creatinine down even while GFR is static or worsening, masking an evolving injury. Cross-check the other signals: is the urine output (weight-indexed, hourly) actually adequate, or has it been under 0.5 mL/kg/h? What is the fluid balance and the trend over several results, not one? Is the underlying driver — sepsis, hypoperfusion, nephrotoxins — actually controlled? If the urine output is poor and the patient is grossly positive, treat the apparent creatinine improvement as an artefact of dilution and keep managing the kidney as at-risk.

audienceQs.q: A patient's eGFR dropped after starting trimethoprim, but they seem well. Is this a real AKI?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Probably not a true fall in GFR. Trimethoprim (like cimetidine and cobicistat) blocks the tubular secretion of creatinine, which normally accounts for 10–15% of its clearance. Blocking secretion raises the serum creatinine and drops the calculated eGFR without any change in actual filtration — a reversible 'pseudo-AKI' that resolves when the drug stops. Trimethoprim also competitively raises potassium by blocking the epithelial sodium channel, so check that too. Distinguish it from real injury by the context (well patient, modest rise of ~10–30 µmol/L soon after starting, preserved urine output) and, if you need certainty, a cystatin-C-based estimate will be unaffected by the secretion block.
